content: Any psychiatrists or psychiatric mental health nurse practitioners care to help me? Back in 2012, I saw a psychiatrist for workplace discrimination—a severe form of chronic job stress. On Day 1, I was diagnosed with a depressive disorder and prescribed Cymbalta. Part of my employment discrimination involved repetitive stress injuries that were taking too long to heal. By six weeks, I was offered ECT. The doctor was trying to help me. I declined. I explain why in Operation Mental Health: Practical Lessons on Career Burnout and Recovery. The medication left me emotionally numb. Then came the brain zaps, constipation, metallic taste, and profuse sweating. At the time, I was working as a Lung Transplant Coordinator. Eventually, I had to take leave just to detox from the treatment itself. So let me ask again: What percentage of your patients return to work better after FMLA? What percentage return needing accommodations to perform their jobs? Are you helping them access their workplace rights? Are you documenting when workplace conditions may be contributing to poor health outcomes? Because if we are not measuring return-to-work outcomes, how do we know whether we are helping? Black women. Nurses. Employees experiencing chronic job stress. Ask the questions before accepting a treatment plan. You do not need a psychiatric diagnosis to use FMLA. You need a serious health condition. Workplace discrimination, retaliation, and chronic job stress can have profound effects on health, families, finances, and communities. Three months ago, I asked 10 psychiatrists and psychiatric mental health nurse practitioners a simple question about return-to-work outcomes. #fmla #psych #mentalhealth Three months later, I am still waiting for an answer. content: Are we celebrating too early? ✋ Two years ago I gave birth to my daughter. I received 20 weeks of paid parental leave. Australia's paid parental leave just increased to 26 weeks. And the government is celebrating. 🎉 But if you've lived through postpartum recovery, you know that 26 weeks is not enough time to heal. Here's what the announcement didn't tell you. Paid parental leave in Australia is paid at the national minimum wage. It's fully taxable. And in the middle of a cost of living crisis, for many families it's financially impossible to survive on. And it's not even 26 weeks for mums, because the pool is shared with your partner, a mother's actual maximum is 22 weeks. Postpartum recovery takes at least 12 months. And can take up to two years after birth. Fewer than half of mothers had fully recovered physically, mentally, and functionally at just 3 to 6 months postpartum. There is a reason postpartum depression is rising. There is a reason birth rates are declining. There is a reason women are leaving the workforce. Giving birth is something you need to recover from. And Australia's paid parental leave system is not built around that reality. Yes, 20 to 26 weeks is progress. But we are nowhere near a milestone worth celebrating. Swipe through to see the full breakdown. → How long did it actually take you to feel like yourself again? content: Burnout doesn't just drain your energy. It changes the way you think. When you're burned out, your brain can get stuck in survival mode. You second-guess things you've already done. You struggle to rest because your mind never gets the message that it's safe to slow down. What many people call "overthinking" is often a nervous system that has been under pressure for too long. Burnout isn't just physical exhaustion. It's cognitive overload. It's carrying so much mental weight that even when you stop working, your brain keeps going. At The Burnout Breakdown, we help people recognize these signs for what they are: indicators that their mind and body may need support, recovery, and time to heal. Through education and guidance around resources like FMLA, we help workers understand their options before burnout reaches a breaking point. Because rest isn't a luxury. It's a biological necessity. content: FMLA is one of the most misunderstood workplace protections. Many employees wait until they're completely overwhelmed to explore their options because they believe taking leave means they've failed, fallen behind, or put their career at risk. In reality, FMLA was created for the opposite reason. The Family and Medical Leave Act exists to give eligible employees protected time away from work when serious health conditions make it difficult to continue working. That can include physical health conditions, but it can also include mental health conditions when they meet the legal requirements. FMLA is not quitting. It is not giving up. It is not choosing your health over your future. It is recognizing that protecting your health is protecting your future. One of the most common patterns we see in burnout is people pushing through symptoms long after their minds and bodies have started asking for help. They tell themselves they just need to work harder, be stronger, or wait until things calm down. Often, things don't calm down. The exhaustion grows deeper, recovery becomes harder, and burnout begins affecting every area of life. That is why understanding your rights matters. At The Burnout Breakdown, our mission is to help people navigate burnout with accurate information, education, and support. We help workers understand FMLA eligibility, mental health leave options, workplace protections, and the next steps available to them so they can make informed decisions during some of the most difficult periods of their lives. Because asking questions about FMLA is not a sign that you've failed. It may be a sign that you've been carrying too much for too long. Your health matters. Your rights matter. content: The Republican Megabill's SNAP cuts are hitting under-resourced families hard — and we're seeing it firsthand in the Washington, DC Metro region. Since the bill was signed into law on July 4, 2025, SNAP participation has fallen sharply across the country. The @centeronbudget has built a powerful state-by-state tracker showing exactly who is losing coverage and where (link in bio). In the DMV, the data tells a stark story. SNAP participation has fallen 13% in Virginia. In DC, we anticipate a 10–15% decrease in the coming months as additional cuts and work requirements take effect this summer. All of our farmers markets accept SNAP, and our dollar-for-dollar incentive match, FreshMatch, offers up to $30 per day. Despite that, SNAP spending at our markets is down 21% from January through April 2026 compared to the same period last year. That drop has real consequences: ➡️ Shoppers who lost SNAP benefits face reduced access to fresh, local food — often replaced by nothing at all. ➡️ Shoppers with reduced benefits face harder choices, often steering toward cheaper, less nutritious options. ➡️ Farmers and food producers lose revenue from both SNAP and FreshMatch sales, weakening regional food security. FRESHFARM is fortunate to operate other food access programs — including Produce Plus, in partnership with @DCHealth — that provide additional pathways to fresh food. But no local program can fully absorb the impact of federal policy changes of this magnitude. The harm to individuals, families, farmers, and the local food economy is real and growing. 📣 For those working in food systems and food access: what are you seeing in your communities? Some cannot process the volume of terminations in time to notify people before their benefits are cut off. Parents of children over the age of 14 are now subject to work requirements for the first time. Food banks are already at pandemic demand levels. And the cuts are just getting started. content: Black Trumpet Farm is proud to be a Pledged Living Wage employer through Just Economics of Western NC. Just Economics calculates the actual cost of living in our region — housing, food, healthcare, transportation, childcare — and sets a wage floor based on what it really takes to live with dignity here. content: DoorDash Driver Highlights Impact of Trump's 'No Tax on Tips' Policy After White House Delivery A DoorDash driver who recently delivered a McDonald's order to the White House says she has personally benefited from President Donald Trump's "no tax on tips" policy included in his broader tax and border legislation. Supporters argue the policy helps workers keep more of their earnings and stimulates economic activity. content: "There is not a single state in America where a full-time minimum wage job covers a two-bedroom apartment. Not one. That's not an opinion. That's from the National Low Income Housing Coalition's annual Out of Reach report. And the numbers behind that headline are staggering. The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour. The housing wage needed to afford a modest two-bedroom apartment nationally is $33.63 an hour. That's more than four times the federal minimum wage. To put it another way, a minimum wage worker would need to work 116 hours a week to afford that apartment. There are only 168 hours in a week total. That leaves 52 hours for sleeping, eating, and everything else that makes up a human life. And it gets worse depending on where you live. In California you need $49.61 an hour. Massachusetts $45.90. Even in West Virginia, the most affordable state on the list, you need $18.49 an hour. The federal minimum wage doesn't clear that bar anywhere. Here's the part that doesn't get talked about enough. This isn't just a minimum wage problem. Nearly half of all U.S. renter households are cost burdened, spending more than 30% of their income on housing. Of the 25 most common jobs in America, 18 of them pay median wages that fall below the two-bedroom housing wage. Those 18 occupations employ 74 million people. Nearly half the entire U.S. workforce. This is a middle class problem as much as it's a minimum wage problem. I grew up watching a parent struggle financially. I know what it feels like when the math just doesn't work no matter how hard you try. The gap between wages and housing costs in this country has reached a point where working harder isn't enough to close it for tens of millions of people. That's the part that should make everyone uncomfortable." This isn't about ordinary Israeli people. It's about government priorities and where public resources are being directed. Australians are facing rising rents, soaring mortgages, increasing food prices, and pressure on healthcare and infrastructure. Yet proposals involving free land and support for foreign defence manufacturing are being openly discussed. If free land is available, why not use it for affordable housing? content: This interactive map highlights the inequitable access to universal school meals across the state. There is significant need in schools without access. Nearly one-quarter of the children in these schools are low-income. These are largely communities where poverty is prevalent but less concentrated or high-cost-of-living areas. New York has made great strides in expanding access to free school meals, but without statewide universal meals, too many schools are left to operate means-tested programs that leave hungry children behind.
